content: The Orthodontic Technicians Association (OTA) is a professional organization primarily composed of orthodontic technicians in the United Kingdom. However, its membership extends internationally, with many of its 312 members, including Fellows, Licentiates, Members, Associate Members, and Honorary Members, practicing outside the UK. In 1971, orthodontic technicians in London began meeting to discuss the regulation and improvement of orthodontic technology standards. Bert Aldridge, then the chief orthodontic technician at the Hospital for Sick Children (now Great Ormond Street Hospital), and Len Bradshaw, from King’s College Dental School, initiated the idea of forming an association. On October 11, 1971, Aldridge invited orthodontic technicians to a meeting at Great Ormond Street Hospital, where 13 attendees agreed to establish the association. A steering committee was formed, with Bradshaw as the first chairman and Aldridge as secretary. Other committee members included P. Chittenden, H. Close, J. Ford, J. Griffin, and H. Haringman. By March 1972, the committee had drafted aims and objectives and sent out letters and questionnaires to dental schools, hospital orthodontic departments, and dental laboratories. To fund the association’s launch, committee members and supporters contributed to a fund for stationery, printing, and postage. Membership applications were invited in July 1972, and the first conference was planned for April 1973. The OTA council meets at the British Orthodontic Society headquarters in London, which opened in 2006. The association’s logo is circular, featuring the letters OTA and an otter, chosen as the mascot due to the phonetic similarity between OTA and otter. The logo is encircled by the words Orthodontic Technicians Association. The OTA’s mission remains aligned with its founders’ goals: to promote the study and advancement of orthodontic laboratory and clinical techniques, ensuring high standards of practice for the benefit of both the orthodontic team and patients. The association advises institutions and individuals on orthodontic laboratory techniques and services. Membership is divided into several categories: Student Members: Dental technicians in training or students interested in orthodontics. They pay reduced fees, receive the journal, and can attend meetings but lack voting rights at the Annual General Meeting (AGM). Associate Members: Individuals with a special interest in orthodontics. They receive newsletters and can attend conferences but cannot vote at the AGM. Members: Qualified dental technicians working in orthodontics without a specialist qualification. They can vote at the AGM, receive newsletters, and attend conferences. Members may use the post-nominal MOTA and stand for election to the council (limited to two members). Licentiates: Members with advanced orthodontic qualifications, such as a City & Guilds Advanced Certificate in Orthodontics or equivalent. Licentiates have the same rights as Members but can also stand for council elections and use the post-nominal LOTA. Honorary Members and Fellows: These titles are awarded at the council’s discretion. Retired Members: Retired members pay reduced fees but retain full access to meetings, conferences, and publications. The OTA organizes several events, including its annual conference, which is considered essential for staying updated on advancements in orthodontic technology. The 2008 conference was scheduled to take place in Edinburgh. The OTA also participates in the British Orthodontic Conference (BOC) and the Dental Technology Show (DTS). The association offers awards to encourage excellence in orthodontic technology: British Orthodontic Society Technicians Award: Established in 1999, this award includes completing a technical project, creating a free-choice appliance, and writing an essay. It is open to students and recently qualified technicians. BOS Award for Distinguished Service: Recognizes exceptional contributions by orthodontic technicians. Aldridge Medal: Introduced in 2007 through a donation by Bert Aldridge, this award is given for the best lecture presented at the annual conference. The inaugural medal was awarded to Susan Owen in 2008. The OTA Council governs the association and is elected by its members. Council members serve voluntarily and represent various regions, including London, the South East, East Midlands, North West, Wales, Scotland, and Ireland. The council also liaises with organizations such as the British Orthodontic Society, the General Dental Council, and educational advisory boards. In 2002, the OTA council gained media attention when members were featured on the BBC News website wearing kilts during a conference in Stirling.
